Header: Brevicoryne brassicae Cabbage aphid in English, Inda in Kinyarwanda language

Prevention: Buy and plant seeds coated with systemic insecticides to protect cabbage seedlings from aphids (see direct control yellow).
Intercrop with aphid- repellent crops (such as pepper, onion, Leek, Geranium) for reducing aphid attack on cabbage.
Conserve natural enemies of aphids through planting or maintaining borders of cabbage field with flowers to provide shelter, food, alternative hosts.
Use mulch and apply compost for providing food for some natural enemies such as predatory beetles.
Avoid nitrogen overfertilization for reducing aphid attack.
Regularly remove weeds to reduce aphid populations.
Monitoring: Monitor the cabbage field once a week during the whole growing season.
Inspect 3-5 consecutive plants at 10 randomly chosen spots of the field.
Look on the underside of leaves where aphids hide.
Look for greyish small insects (2-2.5mm) that are often in colonies and covered by a grey wax.
Action should be taken when 40-50 aphids are seen on more than 20% of inspected plants.
If infected cabbages are close to maturation (firm heads), then action may not be needed anymore.
When scouting check for aphid “mummies” that indicate natural enemy presences (parasitoids).
If many found, no chemical action is needed.
Direct Control: Spray cabbage with botanicals such as: neem oil (7%), or horticultural oil 10% or garlic extract (85g of chopped garlic) per 9l of water, a mixture of garlic, soap and water can also be used
Apply ash in case of a small plot (evenly distributed across leaves)
Use sprinkler irrigation to wash off aphids, but only if no cases of black rot disease were found.
Foliar application, Organophosphate, Contact; IRAC group 1B Imidacloprid.
